name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_CHEMISTRY_UNIT3_MCQI_Q01 - Increasing ionic radii of isoelectronic species

questiontext.text: Consider the isoelectronic species, \(\mathrm{Na}^{+}\), \(\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}\), \(\mathrm{F}^{-}\) and \(\mathrm{O}^{2-}\). The correct order of increasing length of their radii is ________.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Isoelectronic species are atoms or ions that possess the exact same number of electrons. In an isoelectronic series, the ionic radius decreases as the nuclear charge (atomic number, \(Z\)) increases, because a greater positive charge in the nucleus pulls the same number of electrons closer.

Step 2: Evaluation
Each of the given species has \(10\) electrons: \(\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}\) (\(Z = 12\)), \(\mathrm{Na}^{+}\) (\(Z = 11\)), \(\mathrm{F}^{-}\) (\(Z = 9\)), and \(\mathrm{O}^{2-}\) (\(Z = 8\)). Since nuclear charge decreases in the order \(\mathrm{Mg}^{2+} > \mathrm{Na}^{+} > \mathrm{F}^{-} > \mathrm{O}^{2-}\), the effective nuclear attraction on the valence electrons decreases in the same order, causing the ionic radius to increase.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct order of increasing ionic radii is \(\mathrm{Mg}^{2+} < \mathrm{Na}^{+} < \mathrm{F}^{-} < \mathrm{O}^{2-}\).

name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_CHEMISTRY_UNIT3_MCQI_Q02 - Identifying the element that is not an actinoid

questiontext.text: Which of the following is not an actinoid?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In the modern periodic table, the \(f\)-block elements are divided into two series: lanthanoids (atomic numbers \(Z = 58\) to \(71\), where \(4f\)-orbitals are filled) and actinoids (atomic numbers \(Z = 90\) to \(103\), where \(5f\)-orbitals are filled).

Step 2: Evaluation
Checking the atomic numbers of the given elements: Uranium (\(Z = 92\)), Curium (\(Z = 96\)), and Californium (\(Z = 98\)) all fall within the range \(90\) to \(103\) and are actinoids. Terbium (\(Z = 65\)) falls within the range \(58\) to \(71\) and belongs to the lanthanoid series.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Terbium (\(Z = 65\)) is not an actinoid.

name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_CHEMISTRY_UNIT3_MCQI_Q03 - Order of screening effect of s p d f orbitals

questiontext.text: The order of screening effect of electrons of \(s\), \(p\), \(d\) and \(f\) orbitals of a given shell of an atom on its outer shell electrons is:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The screening (shielding) effect of an orbital on outer-shell electrons depends on its penetration power toward the nucleus. Orbitals that are more spherical and penetrate closer to the nucleus shield the outer electrons more effectively from the nuclear charge.

Step 2: Evaluation
For a given principal quantum number \(n\), the \(s\)-orbital is spherically symmetrical and has the highest probability density near the nucleus, followed by \(p\), \(d\), and \(f\) orbitals, which are progressively more diffused.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The order of screening effect is \(s > p > d > f\).

name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_CHEMISTRY_UNIT3_MCQI_Q04 - First ionisation enthalpies of Na Mg Al and Si

questiontext.text: The first ionisation enthalpies of \(\mathrm{Na}\), \(\mathrm{Mg}\), \(\mathrm{Al}\) and \(\mathrm{Si}\) are in the order:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Across a period from left to right, the effective nuclear charge increases and atomic radius decreases, so the first ionisation enthalpy generally increases. However, atoms with fully filled or half-filled subshells exhibit extra stability, and \(s\)-electrons experience greater nuclear attraction than \(p\)-electrons of the same shell due to higher penetration.

Step 2: Evaluation
The valence electronic configurations of the third-period elements are \(\mathrm{Na}\): \(3s^1\), \(\mathrm{Mg}\): \(3s^2\), \(\mathrm{Al}\): \(3s^2 3p^1\), and \(\mathrm{Si}\): \(3s^2 3p^2\). Removing an electron from the fully filled, more penetrating \(3s^2\) subshell of \(\mathrm{Mg}\) requires more energy than removing the single, less penetrating \(3p^1\) electron of \(\mathrm{Al}\). Meanwhile, \(\mathrm{Na}\) has the lowest and \(\mathrm{Si}\) has the highest first ionisation enthalpy among the four.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct order of first ionisation enthalpies is \(\mathrm{Na} < \mathrm{Mg} > \mathrm{Al} < \mathrm{Si}\).

name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_CHEMISTRY_UNIT3_MCQI_Q05 - Electronic configuration of gadolinium Z 64

questiontext.text: The electronic configuration of gadolinium (Atomic number \(64\)) is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Gadolinium (\(\mathrm{Gd}\), \(Z = 64\)) is a lanthanoid (\(4f\)-block element). After the xenon core \([\mathrm{Xe}]\) (\(54\) electrons), there are \(10\) remaining electrons to be distributed among the \(4f\), \(5d\), and \(6s\) orbitals.

Step 2: Evaluation
Two electrons occupy the \(6s\) orbital (\(6s^2\)). Instead of placing all remaining \(8\) electrons into the \(4f\) orbital, one electron enters the \(5d\) orbital so that the \(4f\) subshell attains an exactly half-filled \(4f^7\) configuration, which provides extra exchange-energy stability.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The ground-state electronic configuration of gadolinium is \([\mathrm{Xe}]\,4f^7\,5d^1\,6s^2\).

name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_CHEMISTRY_UNIT3_MCQI_Q06 - Incorrect statement regarding periodic classification of elements

questiontext.text: The statement that is not correct for periodic classification of elements is:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
According to the modern periodic law and the Aufbau principle, electrons fill atomic orbitals in order of increasing \((n + l)\) values. For \(4s\), \(n + l = 4 + 0 = 4\); for \(3d\), \(n + l = 3 + 2 = 5\). Thus, the \(4s\)-orbital has lower energy than the \(3d\)-orbital and is filled first.

Step 2: Evaluation
Properties of elements are indeed a periodic function of their atomic numbers, metallic elements outnumber non-metallic elements in the periodic table, and first ionisation enthalpies generally increase across a period. However, for \(3d\) transition elements, electrons fill the \(4s\)-orbital after the \(3p\)-orbitals and before the \(3d\)-orbitals—not the other way around.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The incorrect statement is that for transition elements, the \(3d\)-orbitals are filled with electrons after \(3p\)-orbitals and before \(4s\)-orbitals.

answer.text: The properties of elements are periodic function of their atomic numbers.
Non metallic elements are less in number than metallic elements.
For transition elements, the \(3d\)-orbitals are filled with electrons after \(3p\)-orbitals and before \(4s\)-orbitals.
The first ionisation enthalpies of elements generally increase with increase in atomic number as we go along a period.

name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_CHEMISTRY_UNIT3_MCQI_Q07 - Order of electron gain enthalpy among halogens

questiontext.text: Among halogens, the correct order of amount of energy released in electron gain (electron gain enthalpy) is:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Down a group, atomic size increases and the attraction of the nucleus for an incoming electron decreases, so the amount of energy released upon gaining an electron (magnitude of negative electron gain enthalpy) generally decreases from top to bottom.

Step 2: Evaluation
Among halogens, \(\mathrm{Cl} > \mathrm{Br} > \mathrm{I}\) follows the expected trend. However, fluorine (\(\mathrm{F}\)) releases less energy than chlorine (\(\mathrm{Cl}\)) because the incoming electron enters the compact \(2p\) subshell of fluorine, where strong inter-electronic repulsion reduces the net energy released compared to the larger \(3p\) subshell of chlorine.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct order of energy released in electron gain among halogens is \(\mathrm{F} < \mathrm{Cl} > \mathrm{Br} > \mathrm{I}\).

name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_CHEMISTRY_UNIT3_MCQI_Q08 - Period number in long form of periodic table

questiontext.text: The period number in the long form of the periodic table is equal to

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In the long form of the periodic table, each horizontal row (period) corresponds to the filling of a new principal energy shell.

Step 2: Evaluation
The period number of an element indicates the highest principal quantum number (\(n\)) of the electrons present in the ground-state atom of that element (or any element in that period).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The period number in the long form of the periodic table is equal to the maximum Principal quantum number of any element of the period.

answer.text: magnetic quantum number of any element of the period.
atomic number of any element of the period.
maximum Principal quantum number of any element of the period.
maximum Azimuthal quantum number of any element of the period.

name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_CHEMISTRY_UNIT3_MCQI_Q09 - Elements with electrons progressively filled in 4f orbital

questiontext.text: The elements in which electrons are progressively filled in \(4f\)-orbital are called

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The \(f\)-block elements are classified into two inner-transition series depending on whether the \(4f\)- or \(5f\)-orbitals are being progressively filled.

Step 2: Evaluation
Elements in which electrons are progressively filled in the \(4f\)-orbital (from Cerium, \(Z = 58\), to Lutetium, \(Z = 71\)) are called lanthanoids. Those filling the \(5f\)-orbital are actinoids, \(d\)-orbital fillers are transition elements, and Group \(17\) elements are halogens.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Elements in which electrons are progressively filled in the \(4f\)-orbital are called lanthanoids.

name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_CHEMISTRY_UNIT3_MCQI_Q10 - Order of size of I I minus and I plus

questiontext.text: Which of the following is the correct order of size of the given species:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
An anion is always larger than its parent neutral atom because adding an electron increases inter-electronic repulsion while the nuclear charge remains unchanged, lowering the effective nuclear charge per electron. Conversely, a cation is always smaller than its parent neutral atom because removing an electron increases the effective nuclear charge per remaining electron.

Step 2: Evaluation
All three species (\(\mathrm{I}^{-}\), \(\mathrm{I}\), \(\mathrm{I}^{+}\)) have the same nuclear charge (\(Z = 53\)), but \(\mathrm{I}^{-}\) has \(54\) electrons, \(\mathrm{I}\) has \(53\) electrons, and \(\mathrm{I}^{+}\) has \(52\) electrons. Thus, \(\mathrm{I}^{-}\) has the largest radius and \(\mathrm{I}^{+}\) has the smallest radius.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct order of size is \(\mathrm{I}^{-} > \mathrm{I} > \mathrm{I}^{+}\).

name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_CHEMISTRY_UNIT3_MCQI_Q11 - Unfavourable gas phase formation of oxide ion O2 minus

questiontext.text:
The formation of the oxide ion, \(\mathrm{O}^{2-}(\mathrm{g})\), from oxygen atom requires first an exothermic and then an endothermic step as shown below:

\[\mathrm{O}(\mathrm{g}) + \mathrm{e}^{-} \longrightarrow \mathrm{O}^{-}(\mathrm{g});\;\Delta H^{\circ} = -141\;\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\]

\[\mathrm{O}^{-}(\mathrm{g}) + \mathrm{e}^{-} \longrightarrow \mathrm{O}^{2-}(\mathrm{g});\;\Delta H^{\circ} = +780\;\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\]

Thus process of formation of \(\mathrm{O}^{2-}\) in gas phase is unfavourable even though \(\mathrm{O}^{2-}\) is isoelectronic with neon. It is due to the fact that,

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Adding a second electron to a negatively charged ion (\(\mathrm{O}^{-}\)) requires overcoming strong electrostatic repulsion between the existing negative charge on the ion and the incoming electron.

Step 2: Evaluation
Although \(\mathrm{O}^{2-}\) attains the noble gas configuration of neon (\(1s^2 2s^2 2p^6\)), the energy required to overcome the inter-electronic repulsion during the addition of the second electron (\(+780\;\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\)) far exceeds the energy released in the first step (\(-141\;\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\)). Consequently, the overall gas-phase enthalpy change is strongly endothermic (\(+639\;\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The formation of \(\mathrm{O}^{2-}(\mathrm{g})\) is unfavourable because electron repulsion outweighs the stability gained by achieving noble gas configuration.

answer.text: addition of electron in oxygen results in larger size of the ion.
electron repulsion outweighs the stability gained by achieving noble gas configuration.
\(\mathrm{O}^{-}\) ion has comparatively smaller size than oxygen atom.

name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_CHEMISTRY_UNIT3_MCQI_Q12a - Block of element with atomic number 57

questiontext.text:
Comprehension: In the modern periodic table, elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic numbers which is related to the electronic configuration. Depending upon the type of orbitals receiving the last electron, the elements in the periodic table have been divided into four blocks, viz, \(s\), \(p\), \(d\) and \(f\). The modern periodic table consists of \(7\) periods and \(18\) groups. Each period begins with the filling of a new energy shell. In accordance with the Aufbau principle, the seven periods (\(1\) to \(7\)) have \(2\), \(8\), \(8\), \(18\), \(18\), \(32\) and \(32\) elements respectively. The seventh period is still incomplete. To avoid the periodic table being too long, the two series of \(f\)-block elements, called lanthanoids and actinoids are placed at the bottom of the main body of the periodic table.

The element with atomic number \(57\) belongs to

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The block of an element in the periodic table is determined by the type of orbital that receives the differentiating (last) electron in its ground-state electronic configuration.

Step 2: Evaluation
The element with atomic number \(57\) is Lanthanum (\(\mathrm{La}\)). Its ground-state electronic configuration is \([\mathrm{Xe}]\,5d^1\,6s^2\). Since the last electron enters the \(5d\)-orbital rather than the \(4f\)-orbital, it belongs to the \(d\)-block.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The element with atomic number \(57\) belongs to the \(d\)-block.

name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_CHEMISTRY_UNIT3_MCQI_Q12b - Outermost configuration of last element of 6th period p block

questiontext.text:
Comprehension: In the modern periodic table, elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic numbers which is related to the electronic configuration. Depending upon the type of orbitals receiving the last electron, the elements in the periodic table have been divided into four blocks, viz, \(s\), \(p\), \(d\) and \(f\). The modern periodic table consists of \(7\) periods and \(18\) groups. Each period begins with the filling of a new energy shell. In accordance with the Aufbau principle, the seven periods (\(1\) to \(7\)) have \(2\), \(8\), \(8\), \(18\), \(18\), \(32\) and \(32\) elements respectively. The seventh period is still incomplete. To avoid the periodic table being too long, the two series of \(f\)-block elements, called lanthanoids and actinoids are placed at the bottom of the main body of the periodic table.

The last element of the \(p\)-block in \(6\text{th}\) period is represented by the outermost electronic configuration.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Each period ends with a noble gas (Group \(18\)) having a completely filled valence \(p\)-subshell (\(ns^2\,np^6\)), except the first period. In the \(6\text{th}\) period, the orbitals filled in order of increasing energy are \(6s\), \(4f\), \(5d\), and \(6p\).

Step 2: Evaluation
The last element of the \(6\text{th}\) period (and of its \(p\)-block) is Radon (\(\mathrm{Rn}\), \(Z = 86\)). Completing the \(6s\), \(4f\), \(5d\), and \(6p\) subshells gives the outermost configuration \(4f^{14}\,5d^{10}\,6s^2\,6p^6\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The outermost electronic configuration of the last element of the \(p\)-block in the \(6\text{th}\) period is \(4f^{14}\,5d^{10}\,6s^2\,6p^6\).

name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_CHEMISTRY_UNIT3_MCQI_Q12c - Atomic number not accommodated in long form periodic table

questiontext.text:
Comprehension: In the modern periodic table, elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic numbers which is related to the electronic configuration. Depending upon the type of orbitals receiving the last electron, the elements in the periodic table have been divided into four blocks, viz, \(s\), \(p\), \(d\) and \(f\). The modern periodic table consists of \(7\) periods and \(18\) groups. Each period begins with the filling of a new energy shell. In accordance with the Aufbau principle, the seven periods (\(1\) to \(7\)) have \(2\), \(8\), \(8\), \(18\), \(18\), \(32\) and \(32\) elements respectively. The seventh period is still incomplete. To avoid the periodic table being too long, the two series of \(f\)-block elements, called lanthanoids and actinoids are placed at the bottom of the main body of the periodic table.

Which of the elements whose atomic numbers are given below, cannot be accommodated in the present set up of the long form of the periodic table?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The seven periods of the modern periodic table have capacities of \(2\), \(8\), \(8\), \(18\), \(18\), \(32\), and \(32\) elements respectively.

Step 2: Step-by-Step Working
Summing the maximum number of elements across all \(7\) periods gives:
\[2 + 8 + 8 + 18 + 18 + 32 + 32 = 118\]
Thus, the present set-up of the long form of the periodic table accommodates elements up to atomic number \(118\). Elements with atomic numbers \(102\), \(107\), and \(118\) all lie within \(1\) to \(118\), whereas \(126\) exceeds \(118\) and would require an \(8\text{th}\) period.

Step 3: Check and Final Answer
The element with atomic number \(126\) cannot be accommodated in the present set-up of the long form of the periodic table.

name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_CHEMISTRY_UNIT3_MCQI_Q12d - Electronic configuration of element above Z 43 in same group

questiontext.text:
Comprehension: In the modern periodic table, elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic numbers which is related to the electronic configuration. Depending upon the type of orbitals receiving the last electron, the elements in the periodic table have been divided into four blocks, viz, \(s\), \(p\), \(d\) and \(f\). The modern periodic table consists of \(7\) periods and \(18\) groups. Each period begins with the filling of a new energy shell. In accordance with the Aufbau principle, the seven periods (\(1\) to \(7\)) have \(2\), \(8\), \(8\), \(18\), \(18\), \(32\) and \(32\) elements respectively. The seventh period is still incomplete. To avoid the periodic table being too long, the two series of \(f\)-block elements, called lanthanoids and actinoids are placed at the bottom of the main body of the periodic table.

The electronic configuration of the element which is just above the element with atomic number \(43\) in the same group is _______.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Elements in the same group have analogous valence-shell electronic configurations. Moving one period up in the \(5\text{th}\) period (\(d\)-block) reduces the atomic number by \(18\) and decreases the principal quantum number of the valence \(s\) and \(d\) orbitals by \(1\).

Step 2: Evaluation
The element with atomic number \(43\) (Technetium, \(\mathrm{Tc}\)) lies in Period \(5\), Group \(7\), with configuration \([\mathrm{Kr}]\,4d^5\,5s^2\). The element just above it in Group \(7\) (Period \(4\)) has atomic number \(43 - 18 = 25\) (Manganese, \(\mathrm{Mn}\)). Its electronic configuration is \(1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^6\,3s^2\,3p^6\,3d^5\,4s^2\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The required electronic configuration is \(1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^6\,3s^2\,3p^6\,3d^5\,4s^2\).

name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_CHEMISTRY_UNIT3_MCQI_Q12e - Family of elements with atomic numbers 35 53 and 85

questiontext.text:
Comprehension: In the modern periodic table, elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic numbers which is related to the electronic configuration. Depending upon the type of orbitals receiving the last electron, the elements in the periodic table have been divided into four blocks, viz, \(s\), \(p\), \(d\) and \(f\). The modern periodic table consists of \(7\) periods and \(18\) groups. Each period begins with the filling of a new energy shell. In accordance with the Aufbau principle, the seven periods (\(1\) to \(7\)) have \(2\), \(8\), \(8\), \(18\), \(18\), \(32\) and \(32\) elements respectively. The seventh period is still incomplete. To avoid the periodic table being too long, the two series of \(f\)-block elements, called lanthanoids and actinoids are placed at the bottom of the main body of the periodic table.

The elements with atomic numbers \(35\), \(53\) and \(85\) are all _______.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The noble gases have atomic numbers \(2, 10, 18, 36, 54, 86, 118\). Each element with an atomic number one less than a noble gas belongs to Group \(17\) (the halogen family) with a valence configuration \(ns^2\,np^5\).

Step 2: Evaluation
Atomic numbers \(35\) (Bromine, \(\mathrm{Br}\)), \(53\) (Iodine, \(\mathrm{I}\)), and \(85\) (Astatine, \(\mathrm{At}\)) are each one unit less than the noble gases \(\mathrm{Kr}\) (\(36\)), \(\mathrm{Xe}\) (\(54\)), and \(\mathrm{Rn}\) (\(86\)) respectively. Hence, all three belong to Group \(17\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The elements with atomic numbers \(35\), \(53\), and \(85\) are all halogens.

name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_CHEMISTRY_UNIT3_MCQI_Q13 - Increasing tendency to gain electron from configurations

questiontext.text:
Electronic configurations of four elements A, B, C and D are given below :

(A) \(1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^6\)

(B) \(1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^4\)

(C) \(1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^6\,3s^1\)

(D) \(1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^5\)

Which of the following is the correct order of increasing tendency to gain electron :

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The tendency of an atom to gain an electron increases as it approaches a stable noble gas configuration across a period. Noble gases already have a completely filled valence shell and therefore have the least tendency to accept an electron (positive electron gain enthalpy).

Step 2: Evaluation
Identifying each element from its configuration:
- \(\mathrm{A}\) (\(1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^6\)) is Neon, a noble gas with a stable octet and the lowest tendency to gain an electron.
- \(\mathrm{C}\) (\(1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^6\,3s^1\)) is Sodium, an alkali metal that readily loses an electron rather than gaining one, giving it a very low tendency to gain an electron.
- \(\mathrm{B}\) (\(1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^4\)) is Oxygen, a Group \(16\) non-metal needing \(2\) electrons for an octet, giving it a high tendency.
- \(\mathrm{D}\) (\(1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^5\)) is Fluorine, a Group \(17\) halogen needing only \(1\) electron to achieve a noble gas configuration, giving it the highest tendency among the four.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct order of increasing tendency to gain an electron is \(\mathrm{A} < \mathrm{C} < \mathrm{B} < \mathrm{D}\).

name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_CHEMISTRY_UNIT3_MCQII_Q14 - Elements showing covalency greater than 4

questiontext.text: Which of the following elements can show covalency greater than \(4\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Period \(2\) elements have only \(2s\) and \(2p\) orbitals (four valence orbitals in total) and lack \(d\)-orbitals; hence their maximum covalency is restricted to \(4\). Period \(3\) elements possess vacant \(3d\)-orbitals in their valence shell, allowing them to expand their octet and exhibit covalency greater than \(4\).

Step 2: Evaluation
Beryllium (\(\mathrm{Be}\)) and Boron (\(\mathrm{B}\)) belong to Period \(2\) and cannot exceed a covalency of \(4\). Phosphorus (\(\mathrm{P}\)) and Sulphur (\(\mathrm{S}\)) belong to Period \(3\) and can use their vacant \(3d\)-orbitals to form species with covalency \(5\) or \(6\), such as \(\mathrm{PCl}_5\) and \(\mathrm{SF}_6\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Phosphorus (\(\mathrm{P}\)) and Sulphur (\(\mathrm{S}\)) can show covalency greater than \(4\).

name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_CHEMISTRY_UNIT3_MCQII_Q15 - Groups of elements imparting colour to flame

questiontext.text: Those elements impart colour to the flame on heating in it, the atoms of which require low energy for the ionisation (i.e., absorb energy in the visible region of spectrum). The elements of which of the following groups will impart colour to the flame?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Elements with very low ionisation enthalpies have loosely held valence electrons that can be excited to higher energy levels by the thermal energy of a Bunsen flame. When these electrons return to the ground state, they emit radiation in the visible region, imparting characteristic colours to the flame.

Step 2: Evaluation
Group \(1\) (alkali metals) and Group \(2\) (alkaline earth metals, excluding \(\mathrm{Be}\) and \(\mathrm{Mg}\)) are \(s\)-block metals with the lowest ionisation enthalpies in their respective periods, so they impart characteristic colours to the flame. In contrast, Group \(13\) and Group \(17\) elements have much higher ionisation enthalpies and do not impart colour to a Bunsen flame.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Elements of Group \(1\) and Group \(2\) will impart colour to the flame.

name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_CHEMISTRY_UNIT3_MCQII_Q16 - Sequences containing atomic numbers of only representative elements

questiontext.text: Which of the following sequences contain atomic numbers of only representative elements?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Representative elements (main-group elements) comprise the \(s\)-block (Groups \(1\) and \(2\)) and \(p\)-block (Groups \(13\) to \(18\)) elements. Transition elements (\(d\)-block, Groups \(3\) to \(12\)) and inner-transition elements (\(f\)-block) are not representative elements.

Step 2: Evaluation
Checking each sequence:
- \(3\,(\mathrm{Li},\,\text{Group }1)\), \(33\,(\mathrm{As},\,\text{Group }15)\), \(53\,(\mathrm{I},\,\text{Group }17)\), \(87\,(\mathrm{Fr},\,\text{Group }1)\): all belong to the \(s\)- and \(p\)-blocks.
- \(2\,(\mathrm{He})\), \(10\,(\mathrm{Ne})\), \(22\,(\mathrm{Ti},\,\text{Group }4)\), \(36\,(\mathrm{Kr})\): contains \(22\), which is a \(d\)-block transition element.
- \(7\,(\mathrm{N})\), \(17\,(\mathrm{Cl})\), \(25\,(\mathrm{Mn},\,\text{Group }7)\), \(37\,(\mathrm{Rb})\), \(48\,(\mathrm{Cd},\,\text{Group }12)\): contains \(25\) and \(48\), which are \(d\)-block elements.
- \(9\,(\mathrm{F},\,\text{Group }17)\), \(35\,(\mathrm{Br},\,\text{Group }17)\), \(51\,(\mathrm{Sb},\,\text{Group }15)\), \(88\,(\mathrm{Ra},\,\text{Group }2)\): all belong to the \(s\)- and \(p\)-blocks.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The sequences \(3, 33, 53, 87\) and \(9, 35, 51, 88\) contain atomic numbers of only representative elements.

name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_CHEMISTRY_UNIT3_MCQII_Q17 - Elements gaining one electron more readily in their group

questiontext.text: Which of the following elements will gain one electron more readily in comparison to other elements of their group?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
An element gains an electron more readily when its electron gain enthalpy is more negative. Although electron gain enthalpy generally becomes less negative down a group, Period \(2\) non-metals (\(\mathrm{O}\) and \(\mathrm{F}\)) have unusually small atomic sizes and compact \(2p\) orbitals, leading to strong inter-electronic repulsion that lowers their electron gain enthalpy compared to the Period \(3\) elements directly below them (\(\mathrm{S}\) and \(\mathrm{Cl}\)).

Step 2: Evaluation
- In Group \(16\), Sulphur (\(\mathrm{S}(\mathrm{g})\), \(\Delta_{eg}H = -200\;\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\)) has the most negative electron gain enthalpy, more negative than Oxygen (\(\mathrm{O}(\mathrm{g})\), \(-141\;\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\)) and heavier chalcogens.
- In Group \(17\), Chlorine (\(\mathrm{Cl}(\mathrm{g})\), \(\Delta_{eg}H = -349\;\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\)) has the most negative electron gain enthalpy, more negative than Fluorine (\(\mathrm{F}(\mathrm{g})\), \(-328\;\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\)), \(\mathrm{Br}\), and \(\mathrm{I}\).
- In Group \(1\), Lithium (\(\mathrm{Li}\)) has a slightly more negative electron gain enthalpy than Sodium (\(\mathrm{Na}\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(\mathrm{S}(\mathrm{g})\) and \(\mathrm{Cl}(\mathrm{g})\) will gain one electron more readily in comparison to other elements of their respective groups.

name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_CHEMISTRY_UNIT3_MCQII_Q18 - Correct statements about periodic properties and elements

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Periodic properties such as first ionisation enthalpy, electron gain enthalpy, and atomic radius follow characteristic trends across periods and down groups, alongside well-known physical states of elements at room temperature.

Step 2: Evaluation
- Helium has a completely filled \(1s^2\) shell with the smallest atomic size and no inner-shell shielding, giving it the highest first ionisation enthalpy in the periodic table (\(2372\;\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\)). This statement is correct.
- Chlorine has a more negative electron gain enthalpy (\(-349\;\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\)) than fluorine (\(-328\;\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\)), not less negative. This statement is incorrect.
- Mercury (a metal) and bromine (a non-metal) are both liquids at room temperature. This statement is correct.
- Across any period, atomic radius decreases from left to right due to increasing effective nuclear charge, so the alkali metal (Group \(1\)) has the largest atomic radius in its period. This statement is correct.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct statements are that helium has the highest first ionisation enthalpy in the periodic table, mercury and bromine are liquids at room temperature, and in any period, the atomic radius of the alkali metal is the highest.

answer.text: Helium has the highest first ionisation enthalpy in the periodic table.
Chlorine has less negative electron gain enthalpy than fluorine.
Mercury and bromine are liquids at room temperature.
In any period, atomic radius of alkali metal is the highest.

name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_CHEMISTRY_UNIT3_MCQII_Q19 - Sets containing only isoelectronic ions

questiontext.text: Which of the following sets contain only isoelectronic ions?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Isoelectronic ions are ions that contain the exact same total number of electrons.

Step 2: Evaluation
Counting the number of electrons in each set:
- \(\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}\) (\(28\)), \(\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}\) (\(18\)), \(\mathrm{Ga}^{3+}\) (\(28\)), \(\mathrm{Al}^{3+}\) (\(10\)): different electron counts, not isoelectronic.
- \(\mathrm{K}^{+}\) (\(19 - 1 = 18\)), \(\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}\) (\(20 - 2 = 18\)), \(\mathrm{Sc}^{3+}\) (\(21 - 3 = 18\)), \(\mathrm{Cl}^{-}\) (\(17 + 1 = 18\)): all are ions with \(18\) electrons each, so they are isoelectronic.
- \(\mathrm{P}^{3-}\) (\(15 + 3 = 18\)), \(\mathrm{S}^{2-}\) (\(16 + 2 = 18\)), \(\mathrm{Cl}^{-}\) (\(17 + 1 = 18\)), \(\mathrm{K}^{+}\) (\(19 - 1 = 18\)): all are ions with \(18\) electrons each, so they are isoelectronic.
- \(\mathrm{Ti}^{4+}\) (\(18\)), \(\mathrm{Ar}\) (\(18\), neutral atom), \(\mathrm{Cr}^{3+}\) (\(21\)), \(\mathrm{V}^{5+}\) (\(18\)): \(\mathrm{Cr}^{3+}\) has \(21\) electrons and \(\mathrm{Ar}\) is neutral, not isoelectronic.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The sets \(\mathrm{K}^{+}, \mathrm{Ca}^{2+}, \mathrm{Sc}^{3+}, \mathrm{Cl}^{-}\) and \(\mathrm{P}^{3-}, \mathrm{S}^{2-}, \mathrm{Cl}^{-}, \mathrm{K}^{+}\) contain only isoelectronic ions.

name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_CHEMISTRY_UNIT3_MCQII_Q20 - Orders not agreeing with variation of indicated property

questiontext.text: In which of the following options order of arrangement does not agree with the variation of property indicated against it?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Periodic trends have well-defined exceptions arising from electronic subshell stability (such as half-filled \(p^3\) configurations) and inter-electronic repulsion in compact \(2p\) orbitals.

Step 2: Evaluation
- \(\mathrm{Al}^{3+} < \mathrm{Mg}^{2+} < \mathrm{Na}^{+} < \mathrm{F}^{-}\): These are isoelectronic (\(10\) electrons), and ionic size increases as nuclear charge decreases (\(13 > 12 > 11 > 9\)). This order is correct.
- \(\mathrm{B} < \mathrm{C} < \mathrm{N} < \mathrm{O}\): Nitrogen (\(2s^2 2p^3\)) has a half-filled \(2p\) subshell, giving it a higher first ionisation enthalpy than Oxygen (\(2s^2 2p^4\)). The correct order is \(\mathrm{B} < \mathrm{C} < \mathrm{O} < \mathrm{N}\), so the given order does not agree.
- \(\mathrm{I} < \mathrm{Br} < \mathrm{Cl} < \mathrm{F}\): Chlorine has a more negative electron gain enthalpy than Fluorine due to smaller inter-electronic repulsion in its \(3p\) orbitals. The correct order of magnitude is \(\mathrm{I} < \mathrm{Br} < \mathrm{F} < \mathrm{Cl}\), so the given order does not agree.
- \(\mathrm{Li} < \mathrm{Na} < \mathrm{K} < \mathrm{Rb}\): Metallic radius increases down Group \(1\) as new principal shells are added. This order is correct.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The arrangements \(\mathrm{B} < \mathrm{C} < \mathrm{N} < \mathrm{O}\) (increasing first ionisation enthalpy) and \(\mathrm{I} < \mathrm{Br} < \mathrm{Cl} < \mathrm{F}\) (increasing electron gain enthalpy) do not agree with the variation of the indicated properties.

name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_CHEMISTRY_UNIT3_MCQII_Q21 - Properties having no unit

questiontext.text: Which of the following have no unit?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Quantities defined as energy changes per mole carry energy units (such as \(\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\) or \(\mathrm{eV\,atom^{-1}}\)), whereas relative or qualitative tendencies have no physical units.

Step 2: Evaluation
- Electronegativity is a relative measure of the tendency of an atom in a covalent bond to attract shared electrons; it is dimensionless and has no unit.
- Electron gain enthalpy and ionisation enthalpy are molar enthalpy changes, both expressed in \(\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\).
- Metallic character is a qualitative/relative tendency to lose electrons and form positive ions; it has no unit.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Electronegativity and metallic character have no unit.
